claim: APC is still active in cytoplasmic extracts of quiescent ciliated RPE1 cells.
source: We found that APC is still active in cytoplasmic extracts of quiescent ciliated RPE1, using the canonical APC substrate Securin (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by degradation assay data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 demonstrating securin degradation in cell extracts.

claim: APC subunit 2 (APC2) is localized to the basal body of ciliated cells.
source: Immunostaining showed that APC subunit 2 (APC2) is localized to the basal body of the ciliated cells (Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A), consistent with the previous report that APC is localized to the basal body of motile cilia in the Xenopus epidermis (Ganner et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A, and corroborated by citation to previous work.

claim: APC is localized to the basal body of motile cilia in the Xenopus epidermis.
source: consistent with the previous report that APC is localized to the basal body of motile cilia in the Xenopus epidermis (Ganner et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ganner et al., 2009.

claim: Co-localization of APC2 with dynactin subunit P150 confirms its localization to the mother centriole.
source: Co-localization of APC2 with dynactin subunit P150 (Guo et al., 2006) further confirmed its localization to the mother centriole (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B and 2C).
evidence: Supported by co-localization data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B and 2C, and citation to Guo et al., 2006 for P150 as a mother centriole marker.

claim: The APC co-activator Cdc20 is localized to the basal body of the primary cilium.
source: Furthermore, we found that the APC co-activator Cdc20 is also localized to basal body of the primary cilium (Figure 1B)
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Cdh1 did not show localization to the basal body of the primary cilium.
source: whereas Cdh1 did not show such localization (Figure1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Cdc20 was not observed at the centrosome of cycling interphase non-ciliated cells.
source: Interestingly, Cdc20 was not observed at the centrosome of cycling interphase non-ciliated cells (Figure 1B and Figure1—figure supplement 2D)
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 2D.

claim: Cdc20 is specifically recruited to the basal body during ciliogenesis, rather than generally binding to the interphase centrosome.
source: indicating that Cdc20 is specifically recruited to the basal body during ciliogenesis, rather than generally binding to the interphase centrosome.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that Cdc20 is present at the basal body of ciliated cells but not at the centrosome of non-ciliated interphase cells.

claim: Cdc20 protein levels are dramatically reduced after serum starvation for 24 hr, due to the exit of cells from proliferation.
source: Western blotting showed that Cdc20 protein levels are dramatically reduced after serum starvation for 24 hr, due to the exit of cells from proliferation (Figure 1—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2E.

claim: Cdc20 protein levels were significantly elevated at 48 hr after serum starvation, when >80% of the cells are ciliated.
source: Importantly, Cdc20 protein levels were significantly elevated at 48 hr after serum starvation, when >80% of the cells are ciliated, consistent with the appearance of this protein at the basal body.
evidence: Supported by Western blot data showing Cdc20 levels at different time points during starvation.

claim: Greater than 80% of RPE1 cells are ciliated after serum-starvation for 48 hr.
source: Greater than 80% of RPE1 cells are ciliated after serum-starvation for 48 hr
evidence: Stated as an established characteristic of the RPE1 cell model system.

claim: Disassembly of primary cilia occurs 1–2 hr after re-adding serum.
source: and disassembly of primary cilia occurs 1–2 hr after re-adding serum.
evidence: Stated as an established characteristic of the RPE1 cell model system.

claim: Reduction of APC subunit 2 (APC2) by siRNA significantly increased the length of primary cilia.
source: Reduction of APC subunit 2 (APC2) by siRNA significantly increased the length of primary cilia marked by acetylated tubulin staining (Figure 2A–C).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining and quantification data in Figure 2A–C.

claim: Depletion of Cdc20 by siRNA had no effect on the percentage of ciliated cells.
source: Consistently, the depletion of Cdc20 by siRNA had no effect on the percentage of ciliated cells, but there was a significant increase in the ciliary length (Figure 2D–F).
evidence: Supported by quantification data in Figure 2D–F.

claim: Depletion of Cdc20 by siRNA resulted in a significant increase in ciliary length.
source: Consistently, the depletion of Cdc20 by siRNA had no effect on the percentage of ciliated cells, but there was a significant increase in the ciliary length (Figure 2D–F).
evidence: Supported by quantification data in Figure 2D–F.

claim: Ciliated cells after the knockdown of either APC2 or Cdc20 are still in quiescent stage.
source: Negative Ki-67 staining demonstrated that these ciliated cells after the knockdown of either APC2 or Cdc20 are still in quiescent stage (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by Ki-67 staining data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Knockdown of Cdh1 by siRNA gave no obvious ciliary phenotype.
source: In contrast, knockdown of Cdh1 by siRNA gave no obvious ciliary phenotype (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A showing no change in ciliary length.

claim: A previous study proposed that APC-Cdh1 promote ciliogenesis.
source: This result is contradictory to a previous study proposing that APC-Cdh1 promote ciliogenesis (Miyamoto et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Miyamoto et al., 2011.

claim: Transiently transfected Cdc20-GFP localized to the centrosome of quiescent cells.
source: When we transiently transfected cells with plasmid encoding Cdc20-GFP, we found it localized to the centrosome of quiescent cells, and completely suppressed the formation of primary cilia (Figure 2G,H).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data in Figure 2G,H.

claim: Overexpression of Cdc20-GFP completely suppressed the formation of primary cilia.
source: When we transiently transfected cells with plasmid encoding Cdc20-GFP, we found it localized to the centrosome of quiescent cells, and completely suppressed the formation of primary cilia (Figure 2G,H).
evidence: Supported by quantification data in Figure 2G,H showing reduced percentage of ciliated cells.

claim: The cilium suppression phenotype by Cdc20-GFP overexpression was confirmed by Immunostaining of Arl13b.
source: This phenotype was confirmed by Immunostaining of Arl13b, another specific marker for ciliary axoneme (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Cdc20 negatively controls the length of the primary cilium.
source: These results suggested that Cdc20 negatively controls the length of the primary cilium.
evidence: Inferred from the combined observations that Cdc20 depletion increases ciliary length and Cdc20 overexpression suppresses cilia formation.

claim: Cell-permeable proTAME efficiently inhibits the APC activity through disruption of the association of APC with its co-activators.
source: Previous studies showed that cell-permeable proTAME efficiently inhibits the APC activity through disruption of the association of APC with its co-activators (Zeng et al., 2010; Zeng and King, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Zeng et al., 2010 and Zeng and King, 2012.

claim: The length of preformed cilia was increased from 4µm to 7µm after treatment of fully ciliated quiescent cells with proTAME for 3 hr.
source: The length of preformed cilia was increased from 4µm to 7µm after treatment of fully ciliated quiescent cells with proTAME for 3 hr (Figure 3)
evidence: Supported by quantification data in Figure 3.

claim: Ciliated cells are still in quiescent stage after short-term treatment with proTAME.
source: Negative Ki-67 staining shows that the ciliated cells are still in quiescent stage after short-term treatment with this drug (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by Ki-67 staining data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The activity of APC is required for maintaining the proper length of primary cilia.
source: This result supports the view that the activity of APC is required for maintaining the proper length of primary cilia.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that APC inhibition by proTAME increases ciliary length.

claim: Primary cilia on DMSO-treated control cells significantly shortened and resorbed 4 hr after serum addition.
source: Primary cilia on DMSO-treated control cells significantly shortened and resorbed 4 hr after serum addition.
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 4A,B showing ciliary length and percentage of ciliated cells.

claim: ProTAME treatment delayed the shortening and resorption of cilia after serum addition.
source: ProTAME treatment delayed the shortening and resorption of cilia (Figure 4A,B), demonstrating that APC activity is required for efficient ciliary resorption before the exit of cells from quiescent phase.
evidence: Supported by quantification data in Figure 4A,B.

claim: APC activity is required for efficient ciliary resorption before the exit of cells from quiescent phase.
source: ProTAME treatment delayed the shortening and resorption of cilia (Figure 4A,B), demonstrating that APC activity is required for efficient ciliary resorption before the exit of cells from quiescent phase.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that APC inhibition delays ciliary resorption upon serum stimulation.

claim: Suppression of either Cdc20 or APC2 by siRNA significantly delayed ciliary shortening after serum addition.
source: Suppression of either Cdc20 or APC2 by siRNA also significantly delayed ciliary shortening (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Calcium influx is necessary and sufficient for shortening and resorption of the primary cilium.
source: Calcium influx is known to be necessary and sufficient for shortening and resorption of the primary cilium (Besschetnova et al., 2010; Plotnikova et al., 2012)
evidence: Supported by citations to Besschetnova et al., 2010 and Plotnikova et al., 2012.

claim: ProTAME treatment prevented ciliary shortening induced by Calcium ionophore treatment.
source: and we found that proTAME treatment also prevented ciliary shortening induced by Calcium ionophore treatment (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A and 2B).
evidence: Supported by quantification data in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A and 2B.

claim: APC-Cdc20 at the basal body maintains cilium length of quiescent cells.
source: Based on these results, APC-Cdc20 at the basal body has two related functions: it maintains cilium length of quiescent cells; it is required for shortening and resorption of the cilium.
evidence: Inferred from the combined observations that APC-Cdc20 inhibition increases ciliary length and delays ciliary resorption.

claim: APC-Cdc20 at the basal body is required for shortening and resorption of the cilium.
source: Based on these results, APC-Cdc20 at the basal body has two related functions: it maintains cilium length of quiescent cells; it is required for shortening and resorption of the cilium.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that APC-Cdc20 inhibition delays ciliary resorption upon serum stimulation.

claim: Ube2S keeps APC partially active during mitotic arrest and is required to fully activate APC-Cdc20.
source: Ube2S keeps APC partially active during mitotic arrest and is required to fully activate APC-Cdc20 (Garnett et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Garnett et al., 2009.

claim: Depletion of Ube2S increased the cilium length in quiescent cells.
source: We found that depletion of Ube2S increased the cilium length in quiescent cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 3)
evidence: Supported by immunostaining and quantification data in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: Depletion of Ube2S delayed ciliary shortening and resorption upon serum stimulation.
source: and delayed ciliary shortening and resorption upon either serum stimulation or calcium influx (Figure 4C; Figure 4—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: Supported by quantification data in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Depletion of Ube2S delayed ciliary shortening and resorption upon calcium influx.
source: and delayed ciliary shortening and resorption upon either serum stimulation or calcium influx (Figure 4C; Figure 4—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: Supported by quantification data in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 2C.

claim: The cell utilizes the general processes for regulation of APC-Cdc20 activity for both mitosis and ciliogenesis.
source: These data imply that the cell utilizes the general processes for regulation of APC-Cdc20 activity for both mitosis and ciliogenesis.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that Ube2S, a mitotic APC regulator, also regulates ciliary length and resorption.

claim: Aurora-A is a known APC substrate during late mitosis.
source: Aurora-A, a known APC substrate during late mitosis, plays an important role in regulating disassembly of primary cilium (Pugacheva et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Pugacheva et al., 2007.

claim: Aurora-A plays an important role in regulating disassembly of primary cilium.
source: Aurora-A, a known APC substrate during late mitosis, plays an important role in regulating disassembly of primary cilium (Pugacheva et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Pugacheva et al., 2007.

claim: Protein levels of Aurora-A do not decrease upon serum stimulation when APC-Cdc20 is activated.
source: We showed that protein levels of Aurora-A do not decrease upon serum stimulation when APC-Cdc20 is activated (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A), consistent with the previous report (Pugacheva et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and citation to Pugacheva et al., 2007.

claim: During ciliogenesis, Aurora-A is autophosphorylated at S51.
source: This may be explained by previous studies showing that during ciliogenesis, Aurora-A is autophosphorylated at S51 (Plotnikova et al., 2012)
evidence: Supported by citation to Plotnikova et al., 2012.

claim: Autophosphorylation of Aurora-A at S51 protects it from APC-mediated degradation.
source: which protects it from APC-mediated degradation (Littlepage and Ruderman, 2002; Littlepage et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citations to Littlepage and Ruderman, 2002 and Littlepage et al., 2002.

claim: The knockdown of Cdc20 in quiescent cells did not affect Aurora-A protein levels.
source: Accordingly, the knockdown of Cdc20 in quiescent cells did not affect Aurora-A protein levels (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Recent studies indicated that APC may regulate ciliogenesis through degradation of dishevelled protein.
source: It was indicated by recent studies that APC may regulate ciliogenesis through degradation of dishevelled protein (Ganner et al., 2009; Miyamoto et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ganner et al., 2009 and Miyamoto et al., 2011.

claim: Dishevelled is not an authentic substrate of APC.
source: However, both specific ubiquitylation assay and in vitro degradation assay showed that dishevelled is not an authentic substrate of APC (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C and 1D), contradictory to their argument.
evidence: Supported by ubiquitylation and degradation assay data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C and 1D.

claim: Genetic mutation in Nek1 was highly associated with short-rib polydactyly syndrome Type Majewski, a new ciliopathy.
source: Genetic mutation in Nek1 was highly associated with short-rib polydactyly syndrome Type Majewski, a new ciliopathy (Thiel et al., 2011)
evidence: Supported by citation to Thiel et al., 2011.

claim: Nek1 is localized to the basal body region.
source: and Nek1 is localized to the basal body region (Shalom et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Shalom et al., 2008.

claim: Both human and mouse fibroblast cells with Nek1 mutations have cilia with abnormal branched structures.
source: Both human and mouse fibroblast cells with Nek1 mutations have cilia with abnormal branched structures (Shalom et al., 2008; Thiel et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Shalom et al., 2008 and Thiel et al., 2011.

claim: The depletion of endogenous Nek1 by siRNA in serum-starved RPE1 cells generated cilia with branched structures.
source: We found that the depletion of endogenous Nek1 by siRNA in serum-starved RPE1 cells generated cilia with branched structures, revealed by acetylated-tubulin staining (Figure 5A–C and Figure 5—figure supplement 2A)
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data in Figure 5A–C and Figure 5—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Nek1 controls the stability and integrity of axonemal microtubules.
source: indicating that Nek1 controls the stability and integrity of axonemal microtubules.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that Nek1 depletion results in branched ciliary structures.

claim: Nek1 knockdown in proliferating RPE1 cells did not affect the structure of either cytoplasmic-acetylated tubulin in microtubules or centrosomal gamma-tubulin.
source: Nek1 knockdown in proliferating RPE1 cells did not affect the structure of either cytoplasmic-acetylated tubulin in microtubules or centrosomal gamma-tubulin (Figure 5—figure supplement 2C)
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data in Figure 5—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Nek1 has a specific and confined role in ciliogenesis.
source: suggesting a specific and confined role of Nek1 in ciliogenesis.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that Nek1 knockdown affects ciliary structure but not cytoplasmic microtubules or centrosomes.

claim: After serum addition, the branched structure can still be efficiently resorbed.
source: After serum addition, the branched structure can still be efficiently resorbed (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B), consistent with the dynamics of ciliary disassembly, indicating that the branched structure is ciliary axoneme.
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data in Figure 5—figure supplement 2B.

claim: The branched structure is ciliary axoneme.
source: After serum addition, the branched structure can still be efficiently resorbed (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B), consistent with the dynamics of ciliary disassembly, indicating that the branched structure is ciliary axoneme.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that the branched structure can be resorbed like normal cilia.

claim: Nek1 levels decreased after serum stimulation.
source: We found that Nek1 levels decreased after serum stimulation (Figure 5D)
evidence: Supported by Western blot data in Figure 5D.

claim: The degradation of Nek1 could be essential for triggering the destabilization of the primary cilium.
source: suggesting that the degradation of Nek1 could be essential for triggering the destabilization of the primary cilium.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that Nek1 levels decrease after serum stimulation when cilia are resorbed.

claim: Nek1 has a canonical destruction box (RXXLXXXN), the APC recognition motif, right after its coiled-coil domain.
source: Finally, Nek1 also has a canonical destruction box (RXXLXXXN), the APC recognition motif, right after its coiled-coil domain.
evidence: Based on sequence analysis of Nek1 protein.

claim: Nek1 is degraded in HeLa cell extracts, and this degradation can be suppressed by Emi1, a specific APC inhibitor protein.
source: We showed by degradation assays in vitro that Nek1 is degraded in HeLa cell extracts, and that this degradation can be suppressed by Emi1, a specific APC inhibitor protein (Figure 5E).
evidence: Supported by degradation assay data in Figure 5E.

claim: Nek1 is efficiently ubiquitylated by APC in in vitro ubiquitylation assay involving purified APC.
source: Nek1 is efficiently ubiquitylated by APC in in vitro ubiquitylation assay involving purified APC (Figure 5F).
evidence: Supported by ubiquitylation assay data in Figure 5F.

claim: Overexpression of Cdc20 leads to reduction of Nek1 levels in quiescent RPE1 cells.
source: Furthermore, overexpression of Cdc20 leads to reduction of Nek1 levels in quiescent RPE1 cells (Figure 5G).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data in Figure 5G.

claim: Nek1 is an APC substrate.
source: These results validate Nek1 as an APC substrate.
evidence: Inferred from the combined observations that Nek1 has a destruction box, is degraded in an APC-dependent manner, is ubiquitylated by APC, and its levels are reduced by Cdc20 overexpression.

claim: Simultaneous depletion of Cdc20 and Nek1 partially rescued the branched cilia phenotype caused by Nek1 knockdown.
source: Moreover, simultaneous depletion of Cdc20 and Nek1 partially rescued the branched cilia phenotype caused by Nek1 knockdown (Figure 5C)
evidence: Supported by quantification data in Figure 5C.

claim: APC-Cdc20 regulates the stability of ciliary axoneme at least in part through antagonizing Nek1 activity.
source: suggesting that APC-Cdc20 regulates the stability of ciliary axoneme at least in part through antagonizing Nek1 activity.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that co-depletion of Cdc20 and Nek1 partially rescues the Nek1 knockdown phenotype.

claim: The primary cilium has an important role in signaling.
source: The primary cilium has an important role in signaling; defects in structure are associated with a variety of human diseases.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge in the abstract.

claim: Defects in primary cilium structure are associated with a variety of human diseases.
source: The primary cilium has an important role in signaling; defects in structure are associated with a variety of human diseases.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge in the abstract.

claim: The activity of the anaphase-promoting complex (APC) destabilizes axonemal microtubules in the primary cilium.
source: We show that the activity of the anaphase-promoting complex (APC), an E3 that regulates the onset of anaphase, destabilizes axonemal microtubules in the primary cilium.
evidence: Supported by the combined experimental data showing that APC inhibition increases ciliary length and delays resorption.

claim: The metaphase APC co-activator, Cdc20, is specifically recruited to the basal body of primary cilia.
source: Furthermore, the metaphase APC co-activator, Cdc20, is specifically recruited to the basal body of primary cilia.
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data showing Cdc20 localization to the basal body.

claim: Inhibition of APC-Cdc20 activity increases the ciliary length.
source: Inhibition of APC-Cdc20 activity increases the ciliary length
evidence: Supported by data showing that Cdc20 knockdown, APC2 knockdown, and proTAME treatment all increase ciliary length.

claim: Overexpression of Cdc20 suppresses cilium formation.
source: while overexpression of Cdc20 suppresses cilium formation.
evidence: Supported by data showing that Cdc20-GFP overexpression reduces the percentage of ciliated cells.

claim: APC-Cdc20 activity is required for the timely resorption of the cilium after serum stimulation.
source: APC-Cdc20 activity is required for the timely resorption of the cilium after serum stimulation.
evidence: Supported by data showing that APC-Cdc20 inhibition delays ciliary resorption after serum addition.

claim: APC regulates the stability of axonemal microtubules through targeting Nek1, the ciliary kinase, for proteolysis.
source: In addition, APC regulates the stability of axonemal microtubules through targeting Nek1, the ciliary kinase, for proteolysis.
evidence: Supported by data showing that Nek1 is an APC substrate and that co-depletion of Cdc20 and Nek1 rescues the Nek1 knockdown phenotype.

claim: These data demonstrate a novel function of APC beyond cell cycle control.
source: These data demonstrate a novel function of APC beyond cell cycle control and implicate critical role of ubiquitin-mediated proteolysis in ciliary disassembly.
evidence: Inferred from the overall findings that APC-Cdc20 regulates ciliary length and resorption.

claim: Ubiquitin-mediated proteolysis plays a critical role in ciliary disassembly.
source: These data demonstrate a novel function of APC beyond cell cycle control and implicate critical role of ubiquitin-mediated proteolysis in ciliary disassembly.
evidence: Inferred from the findings that APC, a ubiquitin E3 ligase, regulates ciliary resorption through targeting Nek1 for degradation.

claim: The primary cilium is highly enriched in receptors for various signaling pathways, including PDGF, calcium, receptor tyrosine kinases, Wnt, and Hh.
source: Though known for over a century, it received little interest until it was appreciated that it is highly enriched in receptors for various signaling pathways, including PDGF, calcium, receptor tyrosine kinases, Wnt, and Hh (Satir et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Satir et al., 2010.

claim: The assembly of primary cilium is coupled to cell cycle exit and entry into quiescence.
source: The assembly of primary cilium is coupled to cell cycle exit and entry into quiescence.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge.

claim: The primary cilium functions as a tumor suppressor organelle that regulates cell proliferation and differentiation.
source: The primary cilium functions as a tumor suppressor organelle that regulates cell proliferation and differentiation (Pan et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Pan et al., 2012.

claim: Dysfunctions of the primary cilium cause a set of human diseases, classified as ciliopathies, such as polycystic kidney diseases.
source: Dysfunctions of the primary cilium cause a set of human diseases, classified as ciliopathies, such as polycystic kidney diseases (Hildebrandt et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hildebrandt et al., 2011.

claim: Cancers are associated with the loss of cilia, due to misregulated cell proliferation through ciliary signaling.
source: Cancers are also associated with the loss of cilia, due to misregulated cell proliferation through ciliary signaling (Plotnikova et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Plotnikova et al., 2008.

claim: Ciliopathies are highly associated with defective ciliogenesis and abnormal ciliary length.
source: Ciliopathies are highly associated with defective ciliogenesis and abnormal ciliary length.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge.

claim: The assembly/disassembly of cilia and maintenance of ciliary length are tightly regulated through control of intraflagellar transport (IFT) and axoneme modification.
source: The assembly/disassembly of cilia and maintenance of ciliary length are tightly regulated through control of intraflagellar transport (IFT) and axoneme modification (Avasthi and Marshall, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Avasthi and Marshall, 2011.

claim: Ciliary length is regulated by the balance of the bidirectional transport of microtubule subunits and associated protein complexes through IFT.
source: Ciliary length is regulated by the balance of the bidirectional transport of microtubule subunits and associated protein complexes through IFT (Pedersen and Rosenbaum, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Pedersen and Rosenbaum, 2008.

claim: The extension/resorption of primary cilia involves changes of the stability of axonemal microtubules, which are controlled by post-translational modifications.
source: Importantly, the extension/resorption of primary cilia also involves changes of the stability of axonemal microtubules, which are controlled by post-translational modifications.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge.

claim: Aurora kinases stimulate disassembly of cilia and flagella by phosphorylation and activation of tubulin deacetylase.
source: For example, Aurora kinases stimulate disassembly of cilia and flagella by phosphorylation and activation of tubulin deacetylase (Pan et al., 2004; Pugacheva et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to Pan et al., 2004 and Pugacheva et al., 2007.

claim: In Chlamydomonas flagella, there is an increase in the levels of protein ubiquitylation during flagellar resorption.
source: In Chlamydomonas flagella, there is an increase in the levels of protein ubiquitylation during flagellar resorption (Huang et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Huang et al., 2009.

claim: Many mitotic regulators have been found to be involved in ciliogenesis, such as Aurora A kinase and NIMA-related kinases.
source: It is curious that many mitotic regulators have been found to be involved in ciliogenesis, such as Aurora A kinase (Pugacheva et al., 2007) and NIMA-related kinases (Moniz et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Pugacheva et al., 2007 and Moniz et al., 2011.

claim: Anaphase-promoting complex (APC) is localized to the basal body of the motile cilia in multiciliated Xenopus epidermal cells, where it has some role in regulating ciliary polarity.
source: Recently, it was shown that anaphase-promoting complex (APC), the key ubiquitin E3 ligase that governs cell cycle progression is localized to the basal body of the motile cilia in multiciliated Xenopus epidermal cells, where it has some role in regulating ciliary polarity (Ganner et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ganner et al., 2009.

claim: In mitosis, APC sequentially recruits co-activators (Cdc20 followed by Cdh1) and cooperates with two specific E2s (UBCH10 and Ube2S) to control proteolysis of key regulators of the metaphase to anaphase transition.
source: In mitosis, APC sequentially recruits co-activators (Cdc20 followed by Cdh1) and cooperates with two specific E2s (UBCH10 and Ube2S) to control proteolysis of key regulators of the metaphase to anaphase transition (Fujita et al., 2009; Fujita et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Fujita et al., 2009.

claim: APC has a less well understood role in regulating other cellular processes, such as neurogenesis, metabolism, and myogenesis.
source: APC also has a less well understood role in regulating other cellular processes, such as neurogenesis, metabolism, and myogenesis (Kim et al., 2009; Eguren et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kim et al., 2009 and Eguren et al., 2011.

claim: Regulation of phosphorylation of APC subunits and Cdc20 is essential for the timing of APC activation during mitotic progression.
source: Regulation of phosphorylation of APC subunits and Cdc20 is essential for the timing of APC activation during mitotic progression (Kramer et al., 2000)
evidence: Supported by citation to Kramer et al., 2000.

claim: APC-Cdc20 is modulated by its inhibitor proteins.
source: APC-Cdc20 is also modulated by its inhibitor proteins (Luo et al., 2000; Madgwick et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to Luo et al., 2000 and Madgwick et al., 2006.

claim: Protein levels of APC cognate E2s, UBCH10 and Ube2S are crucial for the activation of APC-Cdc20, and play a role in the override of mitotic arrest.
source: In addition, protein levels of APC cognate E2s, UBCH10 and Ube2S are crucial for the activation of APC-Cdc20, and play a role in the override of mitotic arrest (Reddy et al., 2007; Garnett et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Reddy et al., 2007 and Garnett et al., 2009.

claim: APC-Cdc20 is localized to the centrosome of postmitotic neurons and plays an important role in dendrite morphogenesis.
source: It was recently found that APC-Cdc20 is localized to the centrosome of postmitotic neurons and plays an important role in dendrite morphogenesis (Kim et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kim et al., 2009.

claim: APC is localized to the basal body of primary cilia of human epithelial cells, where it negatively controls the length and stability of the axonemal microtubules.
source: The APC is localized to the basal body of primary cilia of human epithelial cells, where it negatively controls the length and stability of the axonemal microtubules.
evidence: Supported by the combined experimental data showing APC localization and effects of APC inhibition on ciliary length.

claim: During exit from the quiescent (G0) state APC-Cdc20 is activated and drives ciliary resorption.
source: During exit from the quiescent (G0) state APC-Cdc20 is activated and drives ciliary resorption.
evidence: Supported by data showing that APC-Cdc20 inhibition delays ciliary resorption after serum stimulation.

claim: APC-Cdc20 counteracts the Nek1 activity to regulate the stability of the ciliary axoneme during maintenance and resorption of cilia.
source: Furthermore, our data show that APC-Cdc20 counteracts the Nek1 activity to regulate the stability of the ciliary axoneme during maintenance and resorption of cilia.
evidence: Supported by data showing that Nek1 is an APC substrate and that co-depletion of Cdc20 and Nek1 rescues the Nek1 knockdown phenotype.

claim: The function of Nek1 is to stabilize axonemal microtubules.
source: An explanation for this phenotype is that the function of Nek1 is to stabilize axonemal microtubules.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that Nek1 depletion leads to branched ciliary structures.

claim: Depletion of Nek1 leads to the destabilization and disassembly of axonemal subunits.
source: Thus, depletion of Nek1 leads to the destabilization and disassembly of axonemal subunits.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that Nek1 depletion results in branched ciliary structures.

claim: The disassembled axonemal subunits cannot be transported out of cilia efficiently, and instead they are randomly reassembled in the ciliary lumen, resulting in branched and frayed structures.
source: It would appear that the disassembled axonemal subunits cannot be transported out of cilia efficiently, and instead they are randomly reassembled in the ciliary lumen, resulting in branched and frayed structures.
evidence: Speculative explanation for the branched ciliary phenotype observed upon Nek1 depletion.

claim: Depletion of Nek1 results in defects in ciliary signaling, revealed by the absence of Arl13b staining.
source: Depletion of Nek1 also results in defects in ciliary signaling, revealed by the absence of Arl13b staining (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Proper regulation of APC-Cdc20 activity is essential for normal cellular signaling through primary cilia.
source: This indicates that proper regulation of APC-Cdc20 activity is also essential for normal cellular signaling through primary cilia.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that Nek1 depletion, which is regulated by APC-Cdc20, results in defects in ciliary signaling.

claim: APC may control the degradation of a series of ciliary proteins besides Nek1.
source: We note that APC may control the degradation of a series of ciliary proteins besides Nek1, as this E3 ligase does during mitosis.
evidence: Speculative statement based on the known behavior of APC in mitosis.

claim: The regulation of APC activity during mitosis and meiosis is controlled by the activity of kinases, such as Cdk1.
source: The regulation of APC activity during mitosis and meiosis is controlled by the activity of kinases, such as Cdk1 (Kramer at al., 2000; Madgwick et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kramer et al., 2000 and Madgwick et al., 2006.

claim: Suppression of Cdk activity increased the ciliary length.
source: Our preliminary data showed that suppression of Cdk activity increased the ciliary length (unpublished data)
evidence: Stated as unpublished preliminary data.

claim: The primary cilium is thought to be a concentrated signaling system whose length may act as a rheostat controlling a complement of signaling activities in cells.
source: The primary cilium is thought to be a concentrated signaling system whose length may therefore act as a rheostat controlling a complement of signaling activities in cells.
evidence: Stated as a conceptual framework based on established knowledge.

claim: An understanding of the central role of the APC in control of ciliary length could aid in the identification of new drug targets that may have broad applicability.
source: An understanding of the central role of the APC in control of ciliary length could aid in the identification of new drug targets that may have broad applicability.
evidence: Speculative statement about potential therapeutic applications.
